topic: The Collision-Pi Connection: How Bouncing Blocks Calculate the Circle Constant
target_audience: High school students and undergraduate students interested in the intersection of physics and mathematics.

sections.title: The Setup: A Simple Counting Game
sections.content: Introduce the physical environment: a frictionless floor, a fixed wall on the left, and two blocks of varying masses. A smaller block sits between the wall and a larger block moving toward it. We define the goal: count every single collision (block vs. block and block vs. wall) until the blocks fly away from each other forever.
sections.example: Visualize a tiny 'Mouse' block (mass m) and a giant 'Elephant' block (mass M) on a slide. The Elephant pushes toward the Mouse, which is trapped against a wall.

sections.title: The Pattern: A Mysterious Sequence
sections.content: Present the data for different mass ratios. When the masses are equal (1:1), we get 3 hits. When the ratio is 1:100, we get 31 hits. When it's 1:10,000, we get 314 hits. The pattern emerges: as the mass ratio increases by powers of 100, the digits of Pi (π) appear in the collision count.
sections.example: A digital counter above the blocks flashes '3', then '31', then '314' as we swap the Elephant for a 'Blue Whale' block and then a 'Mountain' block.

sections.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Conservation Laws
sections.content: Explain the two fundamental rules governing these elastic collisions: Conservation of Momentum and Conservation of Energy. Show how the total energy (1/2 mv² + 1/2 MV²) remains constant, acting as a constraint on the velocities of both blocks.
sections.example: Animated graphs showing kinetic energy as a 'budget' that the two blocks must share, never spending more than they have.

sections.title: Mapping to Geometry: The Velocity Space
sections.content: Introduce the 'Phase Space' concept. Instead of looking at the blocks moving on a line, we plot their velocities (v and V) as coordinates on a 2D plane. Because energy is conserved, the possible velocities must lie on an ellipse.
sections.example: A coordinate system where the x-axis is the Mouse's speed and the y-axis is the Elephant's speed. Every collision moves a point from one spot on the curve to another.

sections.title: The 'Circle' Trick: Scaling the Axes
sections.content: Explain how we can transform the energy ellipse into a perfect circle by scaling the velocity axes by the square root of their masses. This mathematical 'stretch' simplifies the physics into pure geometry.
sections.example: An animation showing the ellipse being 'squashed' horizontally until it becomes a perfect circle, making the math much easier to visualize.

sections.title: Collisions as Arc Segments
sections.content: Demonstrate that each collision corresponds to a jump along the arc of this circle. The 'distance' of each jump is determined by the mass ratio. The total number of collisions is simply how many times these jumps can fit into the circle's circumference (2π) before the point leaves the 'collision zone'.
sections.example: Visualize a laser beam bouncing inside a circular mirror. Each time the beam hits the edge, it represents a physical collision of the blocks.

sections.title: Conclusion: The Universal Language
sections.content: Summarize how a linear physics problem is actually a hidden circular geometry problem. The reason π appears is that the laws of conservation naturally describe a circle in the space of possibilities.
sections.example: The camera zooms out from the blocks to show they are moving along a path that traces the digits of π on a giant chalkboard, bridging the gap between physics and pure geometry.
